extracted.intended_audience: reformers, legislators, political theorists, and educated readers interested in designing representative government
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical guidance for structuring suffrage, vote-weighting, methods of election (direct vs. indirect), and mode of voting (secret vs. public) in representative constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural voting justified by mental superiority (not property)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only thing which can justify reckoning one person's opinion as equivalent to more than one is individual mental superiority; plurality of votes may be accorded on the ground of superior education or ability, not on pecuniary qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plural votes should be conferred on grounds of individual mental superiority (education/ability). Property is an imperfect and odious test and should not be the basis. Any scheme must avoid grounding plurality in mere pecuniary circumstances because that compromises principle and public acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property must not be the basis for electoral privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: It is entirely inadmissible, unless as a temporary makeshift, that the superiority of influence should be conferred in consideration of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although property correlates imperfectly with education, tying plurality to pecuniary qualifications is objectionable and will make permanent maintenance impracticable. Property-based plural voting both offends sentiment and risks corrupting the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation as a practical proxy test for intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of trustworthy general examinations, the nature of a person's occupation is some test of intelligence; employers, foremen, skilled tradespeople, bankers, merchants and manufacturers are on average more intelligent than ordinary laborers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use occupation as an approximate test only where sustained successful performance (not mere nominal status) is required; to prevent nominal qualification, require occupation to have been exercised for a period (suggested example: three years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal professions and graduates as grounds for higher vote-weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the liberal professions, where really and not nominally practiced, and graduates of universities imply a higher degree of instruction and could be admitted at once to a plurality of votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where entrance to a profession requires sufficient examination or serious educational conditions, its members can be given extra votes. University graduates and holders of valid certificates from higher schools may be registered and accorded plurality subject to safeguards that teaching/examination are genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary examinations/certificates open to all as a route to plurality
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be voluntary examinations at which any person whatever might present himself, prove that he meets the standard of knowledge and ability, and be admitted to plurality of votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create fair, open examinations (e.g., Oxford 'associate' local exams or equivalents) and accept satisfactory certificates of study under securities that the teaching is real, not a pretense. The route must be genuinely open so the poorest can claim the privilege by direct proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural voting must not let privileged classes outweigh the rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Plurality of votes must on no account be carried so far that those who are privileged by it, or the class to which they chiefly belong, shall outweigh by means of it all the rest of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design gradations and distinctions so they are not arbitrary and are comprehensible and acceptable by general conscience; ensure aggregate weight of privileged voters cannot dominate policy or enact 'class legislation'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow registration-based plural votes for graduates/professionals across constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Reform Bill that lowers pecuniary conditions, it might be wise to allow graduates of universities, persons who passed higher schools, and members of the liberal professions to be registered specifically and give their votes as such in any constituency they choose to register, while retaining their simple citizen vote locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a registration mechanism that permits professionals/graduates to exercise a plurality-vote status in constituencies of choice, without removing their ordinary local citizen vote; this can extend privilege while tying it to demonstrable qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional representation as remedy to universal equal suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal and universal suffrage may produce evils unless made real by proportional representation of all minorities (Mr. Hare's principle); proportional representation could make universal suffrage acceptable by securing minorities' representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If universal suffrage is adopted, include a system of proportional representation to ensure minorities are proportionally returned and thus prevent domination by a simple majority. Note: some plural schemes are incompatible with Hare's intercommunity requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage (indirect) election is generally inferior to direct election
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing representatives by a double process (primary electors choosing electors who then elect MPs) reduces the cultivation of public spirit and political intelligence, risks corruption, and often merely reproduces direct-election results without the benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect election works poorly because primary electors tend to vote for pledged electors/partisan lists; it creates a superfluous middle wheel, weakens the member's sense of responsibility to constituents, concentrates bribery opportunities, and should be avoided unless special conditions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect election acceptable only when electors have other important functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect election answers well when electors are elected for other important local/national functions (e.g., U.S. Senate chosen by State Legislatures) so that they exercise judgment with reference to those duties rather than merely as delegates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indirect election only where the intermediary body has substantial unrelated responsibilities (municipalities or legislatures), making them suitable judges for national office; avoid creating bodies chosen solely to be electors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral systems should cultivate public spirit and political intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary purpose of giving the franchise is to develop public spirit and political intelligence among voters; modes of election should promote interest and exercise of faculties in public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer mechanisms that engage voters directly (direct election, meaningful participation) over arrangements that render participation perfunctory or delegatory; avoid devices that discourage voters from caring about final results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public (open) voting is the default for political affairs; secrecy is exceptional
rubrics_metrics.description: Secrecy in voting is justifiable in many cases and imperative in some, but in affairs of a political character secrecy should be the exception; the spirit of the institution matters—public voting fosters the conception of the vote as a trust for the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor public voting to reinforce the idea that the suffrage is a trust owed to the public and to cultivate political accountability and the political 'point of honor'. Use secret ballots only where reasonable fear or avoidable evils make secrecy necessary to protect voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy justified where necessary to protect voters from real evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Secrecy is not cowardice; it is justifiable and sometimes imperative to seek protection against evils which are honestly avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize legitimate cases for secret voting—where publicity would expose voters to coercion, intimidation, or other avoidable harms—and permit secret ballots in those instances while treating secrecy as an exception rather than the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffrage must be based on personal conditions, not sex; women entitled to vote
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference of sex is entirely irrelevant to political rights; women have the same interest in good government and require the suffrage no less (arguably more) than men; denying women the vote lacks principle, especially where other personal qualifications are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sex-based disqualifications (as irrational as disqualifying by height or hair color). Where suffrage depends on personal conditions (householder status, tax payment, etc.), women who meet those conditions should not be excluded; enfranchisement benefits women's dignity, household respect, accountability, and the quality of votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffrage exists to prevent misgovernment as much as to enable governance
rubrics_metrics.description: People do not need political rights primarily to govern but to prevent being misgoverned; the suffrage is a protection for all classes, including those permanently occupied in manual labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the franchise to ensure all groups vulnerable to misgovernment can protect their interests; do not withhold suffrage on presumptions about capacity to govern—its value lies in securing protection and preventing abuse by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions should embody a spirit that favors knowledge and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of national institutions shapes national character; institutions should not sanction the creed that ignorance is entitled to as much political power as knowledge, but should profess that the wiser ought to have greater influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing electoral institutions, consider not just legal provisions but their educative/spiritual effect on citizens' self-conception (e.g., whether institutions encourage political responsibility, respect for knowledge, and public-mindedness).
